strengths: The paper addresses an important NLP evaluation problem: whether brain-to-text results demonstrate generalization beyond previously observed subjects and text stimuli.

Distinguishing subject overlap from stimulus overlap is useful. Holding out both is appropriate for the stated goal of decoding unseen text from unseen people, and the discussion recognizes the additional complications of overlapping fMRI windows.

Experiments cover two modalities, Narratives and ZuCo, and two established decoding models. The substantial performance differences across splitting protocols motivate closer scrutiny, while reporting overlap statistics across four seeds is helpful.
weaknesses: The central causal claims exceed the evidence (Section 4.4). Decreasing reconstruction loss or improving BLEU with longer training does not establish encoder degradation or decoder memorization. Random encoder initialization also does not remove information from the input signals. Signal-shuffling, uninformative-input, and decoder-only controls are needed to establish whether accurate generation depends on brain information.

Performance comparisons confound overlap removal with changes in subjects, stimuli, retained data, and optimization. The proposed split discards examples without reporting how many; EEG2Text uses learning rate 1e-4 in Table 3 but 1e-6 for the proposed benchmark in Appendix A. Matched training budgets, retained-data statistics, and controlled comparisons are needed to attribute performance differences specifically to contamination.

The pseudocode does not preserve the proposed disjointness guarantee as written. Algorithm 1, line 15, restores edges based only on subject membership, allowing training subjects to reconnect to test stimuli. Algorithm 2, line 33, checks task membership but can reconnect training tasks to test subjects. Both endpoints must belong to the same partition. This directly affects reproducibility of the paper's principal methodological contribution.

The quantitative reporting requires correction. Equation (7) counts identical recordings shared between training and test sets, whereas the surrounding argument concerns different recordings from shared subjects; these are different quantities. Table 3 also reports ROUGE-1 F=84.64 with P=63.16 and R=71.50, which is inconsistent with standard F1 computation or averaging. The formulas, implementation, and reported results need reconciliation.

The claimed benchmark release is insufficiently documented. Although Appendix A provides some hyperparameters, the manuscript supplies no identifiable code or split-artifact link, exact split membership, retained sample counts, or explicit generation protocol, including whether reference prefixes are supplied. Generation results lack variability across splits or training runs; the four-seed analysis covers overlap statistics only.

The framing should distinguish evaluation objectives. Subject overlap can be legitimate for personalized decoding, although it cannot establish generalization to unseen subjects. The proposed joint holdout is appropriate for the paper's chosen objective, but blanket claims that existing protocols are contaminated or inherently corrupt training are too broad. Together with the missing controls and incorrect split specification, these issues require important revisions before a Findings recommendation.
